public_rationale: Google’s randomized trial of 96 engineers using internal tools in summer 2024 estimated about 21% less task time with AI assistance, with a large confidence interval [e1]. METR’s report, revised July 25, 2025, tested tools described as the February–June 2025 frontier, primarily Cursor Pro and Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet [e2]. Across 246 tasks involving 16 experienced open-source developers, allowing AI increased completion time by 19% [e2]. The productivity benefit holds in Google’s tested setting but does not hold in METR’s experienced-maintainer setting [e1, e2].
limitations: Neither study establishes an industry-wide average effect or isolates autocomplete from other assistance features [e1, e2].
Google cautions that its result may not generalize across tools or periods [e1].
METR’s stated tool period extends beyond the March 12, 2025 claim; the cited abstract does not date individual tasks or provide a separate effect for tools available by that date [e2].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI coding tools, acting as a fantastic, souped-up version of autocomplete, somewhat increase productivity.
conditions: as a souped-up version of autocomplete

statement.excerpt: As a fantastic, souped-up version of autocomplete, AI coding tools somewhat increase productivity.

our_interpretation: Productivity means useful development work completed per unit of time, including time spent checking and correcting suggestions.
Somewhat indicates a positive effect without supplying a numerical ceiling or promising that every developer benefits.
Read autocomplete as a description of human-supervised coding assistance, rather than an exact restriction to a single user-interface feature.
Assess the tool generation surrounding publication. Later reports can inform this causal assessment when they study those tools; this is not a forecast about future agents.
Different effects across credible development settings warrant a mixed finding rather than assuming an industry-wide average.
criteria.support_condition: Controlled comparisons show that human-supervised AI coding assistance reduces completion time or increases completed work at an adequate quality level.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable controlled comparisons show increased completion time or reduced completed work, limiting the general positive claim.

evidence.locator: Abstract; study design in Sections III and IV
evidence.explanation: A randomized study of 96 Google engineers estimated about 21% less task time with completion, paste, and code-generation assistance. The task required passing tests, although the estimate had substantial uncertainty.

Sixteen experienced maintainers completed 246 randomized tasks more slowly when AI was allowed. The study covered February–June tools, primarily Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7; it is adverse evidence for broad coding assistance, not an isolated test of autocomplete.
